extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, and semantics
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and classifying kinds of names/terms in formal and philosophical logic (abstract vs concrete, connotative vs non-connotative, relative, privative, etc.), and guidance on how names should be defined or fixed for clear reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract vs. Concrete names
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'abstract' (in Logic proper) mean the opposite of 'concrete'; an abstract name is the name of an attribute; a concrete name is the name of an object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'whiteness' is an abstract name (the name of the color), 'white' is a concrete name (a name of white objects). Historical note: the author follows the schoolmen's usage and warns that modern usage (e.g., Locke/Condillac) has broadened 'abstract' to include all general names, which the author regards as a misappropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some abstract names are general, others singular (treatment of attribute-names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some abstract names name a class of attributes (e.g., 'color', 'whiteness' used broadly, 'magnitude', 'weight'), while other abstract names designate a single, non-varying attribute (e.g., 'visibleness', 'squareness', 'milk-whiteness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an abstract name denotes a single attribute conceived as one, it is neither properly general nor individual; the author suggests placing such names in a separate class to avoid logomachy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal-use determines what a word names (adjectives vs abstract nouns)
rubrics_metrics.description: A word should be considered the name of that which is intended by its principal use (especially in predication). 'White' in predication names the subjects that have the color and connotes whiteness; 'whiteness' names the attribute itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction explains why adjectives are placed in the concrete class even though they relate to attributes. The author emphasizes looking at how a word is principally used when deciding what it names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative vs. Non-connotative (absolute) names
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-connotative term signifies a subject only or an attribute only; a connotative term denotes a subject and implies (connotes) an attribute. Connotative names indicate that the subjects possess a particular attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'John' or 'London' signify subject only (non-connotative); 'whiteness' signifies an attribute only (non-connotative); 'white', 'long', 'virtuous' are connotative (denote things and connote the corresponding attribute). The author treats this as a fundamental distinction that reaches deep into the nature of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: All concrete general names are connotative
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete general names (e.g., 'man') denote an indefinite class of individuals and, in doing so, imply certain attributes (e.g., corporeity, animal life, rationality, human form) — they connote those attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example discussion: if hypothetical beings had some human attributes but not others (form without reason, or reason without human form), we might not call them 'men' — showing that the connotation (the set of attributes) determines application. The author notes vagueness can arise about exact connotation and that this bears on classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names are not connotative
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names denote individual subjects only and do not indicate or imply attributes as part of their signification; they are essentially marks for identifying individuals rather than conveying information about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: personal names (Paul), place names (Dartmouth). The author gives the chalk-on-house analogy: a proper name functions like a mark to enable identification in discourse but does not itself assert facts about the object. Any historical reason for the name (e.g., father’s name, location) is not part of its signification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some individual names can be connotative (connotative individual names)
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual name may be connotative when its meaning includes an attribute or a relation so determinate that only one individual fits it (e.g., 'the only son of John Stiles', 'the first emperor of Rome').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms for individualization include: grammatical articles ('the'), limiting words ('present'), contextual specification (Cæsar’s army in a particular battle), and multi-word expressions that restrict a general name so it becomes predicable of a single object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of names resides more in connotation than denotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When names convey any information, their meaning resides not in what they denote (the subjects) but in what they connote (the attributes implied). Proper names connote nothing and so strictly have no signification beyond identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: the same individual may bear many names ('Sophroniscus', 'father of Socrates', 'Athenian', 'sculptor', 'honest man'), each conveying different facts to someone who understands the name. One might know all individuals a name applies to and yet not know its meaning (i.e., its connotation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names with indeterminate connotation cause vague thought and must be fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Using connotative terms without a distinctly ascertained connotation leads to vagueness and lax habits of thought; people often apply names by superficial similarity without precise analysis of the connoted attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The remedy is to give every frequently used general concrete name a definite and fixed connotation (i.e., define it) with minimal change to the class of objects it habitually denotes, so as to minimize disruption to existing usage and common propositions. The author warns that failure to do so has especially degraded vocabulary in mental and moral philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity (multiple fixed connotations) differs from indeterminate connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: A word may have several fixed and recognized meanings (ambiguous/equivocal), which are distinct and can be treated as separate names (e.g., 'post', 'box'), whereas indeterminate connotation lacks fixed recognized senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple meanings are fixed and distinguishable, it is often acceptable to retain the same form for different senses, provided they are clearly kept separate. This differs from the problematic case where a connotative term has no clear, agreed connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive vs. Negative names (and negative connotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive names (e.g., 'man', 'good') name the presence of attributes; negative names (e.g., 'not-man', 'not-good') name the absence of attributes. Negative connotative names connote the absence of an attribute (i.e., 'not-white' connotes non-possession of whiteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that form and reality may diverge: words in positive form can express negative realities (e.g., 'idle' meaning 'not working'), and words in negative form can express positive attributes (e.g., 'inconvenient' expresses being a cause of annoyance, not simply the absence of convenience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privative names (hybrid positive/negative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A privative name denotes something that has once had, or might be expected to have, a particular attribute but does not (e.g., 'blind'). It is equivalent in signification to a positive and a negative name taken together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privative names connote two things: the absence of certain attributes and the presence of other attributes (e.g., 'blind' typically applies to beings expected to see and thus implies prior or expected possession of sight). The author distinguishes privative use from mere negation and gives rhetorical contexts where privative meaning applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative vs. Non-relative (relative) names and the fundamentum relationis
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative names (e.g., father/son, cause/effect, longer/shorter) are always given in correlative pairs and, beyond denoting a subject, imply the existence of another object; the attribute they connote is essentially a relation (a series of events or facts involving both parties—fundamentum relationis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative names can be understood as connoting the same underlying fact viewed from different perspectives (e.g., 'A is father of B' and 'B is son of A' assert the same fact). A name is relative when its meaning cannot be explained without mentioning another thing; the author argues this is not mysterious but reducible to ordinary attributes grounded in facts involving multiple objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal, Æquivocal, and Analogical (metaphorical) use of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal when applied in the same sense to all things it predicates of; æquivocal (equivocal) when applied in different senses; analogical (metaphorical) when applied in similar but not identical derived senses (primary and secondary senses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'file' meaning a steel tool vs. a line of soldiers are distinct (æquivocal); 'brilliant' applied to light and achievements shows analogical use. The author emphasizes that an equivocal word is effectively multiple names coinciding in form and that one common fallacy is treating a metaphorical application as if it were literal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness can be tolerable or even useful in classification (with precautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial uncertainty in the connotation of general names can exist without mischief in some contexts; for instance, vagueness may help range borderline species or individuals with nearest resemblance in natural history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such vagueness must be guarded by strict precautions; careless use of connotative terms without ascertained connotation produces lax thinking. The author promises to show conditions under which vagueness is harmless and when it must be eliminated by definition.
